description.narrative:
To deliver on its triple mandate, UN Women should lead issues on gender equality and the empowerment of women, and to promote accountability within the UN system (coordinating mandate), have universal coverage, strategic presence and provide support to intergovernmental policy and normative processes (normative mandate) and carry out programmes at country level (operational mandate).
The intervention will support two thematic areas of UN Women's Strategic Plan, Impact area 1: Increase women's leadership and participation and Impact area 4: to increase women's leadership in peace, security and humanitarian response.
The SPF has four intended outcomes (two per impact area).1.1 Legislation and policies to advance women's rights and promote their participation in decision-making bodies are reformed and adopted.1.2 Gender responsive measures (mechanisms, processes and services) promote women's leadership and participation in politics. 4.1 Women, Peace and Security commitments and accountability frameworks are adopted and implemented in conflict and post-conflict countries.4.2 Gender equality commitments adopted and implemented in humanitarian action which includes disaster risk reduction and preparedness, response and recovery.

UN Women bildades 2010 genom beslut i FN:s generalförsamling och är operativt sedan den 1 januari 2011. UN Women arbetar med jämställdhet och kvinnors ökade egenmakt. UN Women har ett unikt mandat att leda, samordna och främja ansvarsutkrävande för hela FN-systemets arbete för jämställdhet och är sekretariat för FN:s Kvinnokommission (Commission on the Status of Women, CSW). Organisationen arbetar såväl normativt som operativt och ska ej ersätta övriga delar av FN-systemets jämställdhetsarbete. UN Womens målsättning är att uppmärksamma de jämställdhetsdimensioner som finns inom alla utvecklings- och MR-områden. Med utgångspunkt i den vision om jämställdhet som uttrycks i FN-stadgan arbetar UN Women bland annat för eliminering av diskriminering av kvinnor och flickor, kvinnors egenmakt och jämställdhet mellan kvinnor och män som mottagare av utveckling, MR, humanitär hjälp och fred och säkerhet. Organisationen arbetar även med att i samarbete med andra delar av FN-systemet formulera globala standarder och normer samt med att stödja medlemsländerna med implementering av dessa.
UN Women har ansökt till Sida om finansiering för "Strategic Partnership Framework 2017-2020" (SPF) med en total budget på 320 MSEK för fyra år.
Programmet är en fortsättning på det SPF som implementerades under 2011- 2016 med goda resultat. Resultaten bekräftas av en utvärdering av programmet samt en halvtidsöversyn av UN Womens strategiska plan 2014-2017. SPF 2017- 2020 syftar till att stödja UN Women att implementera sin Strategiska Plan 2014-2017 samt den nya Strategiska Planen som kommer att gälla 2018- 2021. Sidas finansiering kommer att gå till följande två resultatområden (Impact areas); 1) Öka kvinnors deltagande och inflytande i beslutsfattande organ; 4) Öka kvinnors ledarskap i fred, konflikt och humanitär respons. Programmet har en global ansats.
Sammanfattningsvis kommer det föreslagna programmet att bidra till: - Öka kvinnors ledarskap och deltagande, genom lagstiftning och policyer som förbättrar kvinnors rättigheter och genom att verka för kvinnors deltagande i beslutsfattande organ, samt genom att öka kvinnors politiska deltagande och inflytande.
- Öka kvinnors ledarskap i insatser för fred, säkerhet och humanitär respons genom att stärka implementeringen av kvinnor, fred och säkerhets åtaganden och ansvarsutkrävande ramverk i konflikt - och post konflikt länder, men även genom att stärka implementeringen av jämställdhetsåtaganden i humanitära insatser. Det bedöms relevant att humanitärt arbete omfattas av stödet då 80% av humanitära kriser sker i konfliktkontexter.
- Stärka UN Womens koordinering av FN systemet och dess partnerskap, resultatbaserade styrning, rapportering, kunskapshantering och utvärdering samt organisatorisk effektivitet på regional - och landnivå.

UN Women has applied to Sida for funding for the "Strategic Partnership Framework 2017-2020" (SPF) with a total budget of 320 million SEK for four years.
The program is a continuation of the SPF that was implemented during 2011-2016 with good results. The results are confirmed by an evaluation of the program and a mid-term review of UN Women's Strategic Plan 2014-2017. SPF 2017-2020 aims to support UN Women to implement its Strategic Plan 2014-2017 and the new Strategic Plan that will apply 2018-2021. Sida's funding will go to the following two impact areas; 1) Increasing women's participation and influence in decision-making bodies; 4) Increasing women's leadership in peace, conflict and humanitarian response. The program has a global approach.
In summary, the proposed programme will contribute to: - Increasing women's leadership and participation, through legislation and policies that improve women's rights and by promoting women's participation in decision-making bodies, as well as by increasing women's political participation and influence.
- Increasing women's leadership in peace, security and humanitarian response efforts by strengthening the implementation of women, peace and security commitments and accountability frameworks in conflict and post-conflict countries, but also by strengthening the implementation of gender commitments in humanitarian efforts.
It is considered relevant that humanitarian work is covered by the support as 80% of humanitarian crises occur in conflict contexts.
- Strengthening UN Women's coordination of the UN system and its partnerships, results-based governance, reporting, knowledge management and evaluation, and organizational effectiveness at regional and country levels.

sector.narrative: Women’s rights organisations and movements, and government institutions

description.narrative:
HIGHLIGHTS OF RESULTS FROM SPF II IN 2021:
SPF IIs outcomes are, since the inception, aligned with the outcomes of UN Womens Strategic Plan 2018-2021. The reporting shows, as previous years, that most indicators have surpassed their targets and it is evident that the program overall has progressed well and will reach most targets at the end of 2021.
UN Women does not report any unexpected results, but does mention the challenge that unexpected political developments and crises during 2021 posed to its planned implementation and expected results.
Apart from specifying a wide range of results within the two areas of WPP and WPS, the report, positively, includes a specific section on key partnerships during the year, as well as a section that highlights new developments, which UN Women sees as key. For example, the CSW65 Agreed Conclusions from 2021 which represent a historic normative advancement since the Member States reaffirm their commitment to women's political participation by setting the highest-ever international target for women's representation (50/50). The commitments urge governments and relevant stakeholders to leave no one behind in addressing the root causes of barriers to WPP by strengthening normative, legal, and regulatory frameworks, gender-responsive institutional reforms, and financing for WPP. UN Women's co-leadership in two pillars of the Secretary General's Call to Action for Human Rights (one on temporary special measures and one on elimination of discriminatory laws) is also mentioned here. Normative advances also included the enhanced focus on political and financial support to gender equality by the Gender Equality Forum in 2021, as a new Compact on WPS was launched and have received 160 signatories (Member states, civil society etc) for various commitments over a five year period. Sida takes note that the global furthering of the agenda is focused on implementation and not new resolutions or likewise. The new UN Women Humanitarian Strategy also marks an important new development.
Women's Political Participation, WPP
Overall: In the SPFII annual report of 2021, the results that relate to women's political participation are outlined within the main narrative report, as well as within the Annex C. Annex C provides an overview of the country-based programming supported by SPFII in 2021. Hence, although such results are covered within the main narrative report, Annex C provides a more detailed and in-depth picture of activities supported in 25 countries in Africa, Latin America and the Middle East. This is a larger number of examples presented than in the 2020 report (2020: 15 countries in the same three regions).
In summary, in 2021, UN Women provided in-country and remote policy guidance, and technical assistance, on WPP including expert deployments, to over 65 countries and six regional offices. Over USD 7,4 million in seed funding were provided to 40 countries and five regional offices. Consequently, legal and policy reforms were ensured, and enhanced WPP occurred in national and local elections in 26 countries. Over USD 200 million were, moreover, catalyzed for WPP programming. Sida sees it as positive that this figure is clearly monitored and presented within this year's report, since the reporting, historically, has merely presented the corresponding figure within the WPS area.
Outcome 1.1: Legislation and policies to advance women's rights and promote their participation in decision-making bodies are reformed and adopted.
Under this outcome, UN Women provides its UN Country Offices, as well as it national partners such as government agencies, electoral stakeholders, networks of women leaders, with technical assistance, as well as provides them with comparative knowledge and tools in order to ensure that policies and legislation, which promote womens political participation (WPP), are reformed, adopted and implemented. It is also under this outcome that UN Women provides its country offices with technical, financial (seed funds) and coordination support in order to ensure the same advances.
The CO offices in Iraq and Mexico are two examples of recipients of SPF seed funds in 2021. In Iraq, UN Women supported the Council of Ministers in Establishing a Supreme Committee (SC) with a mandate to promote women's participation and protection in Oct 2021 parliamentary elections. As the only UN agency nominated to sit on the SC (total 14 members, mostly government agencies), UN Women had a significant opportunity to provide assistance to the SC and its members. E.g. the Independent High Electoral Commission (IHEC), as one of the members, ensured a Electoral Code of Conduct with specific gender equality provisions, including provisions against VAWP. An important result was that all political parties in all governorates, the President, the Prime Minister and the Speaker of the Parliament all signed it. Additionally, that agency, together with the Department of Women's Empowerment (DWE), ensured the development of a training manual that was, subsequently, used by the IHEC and UN Women when they trained polling staff in a training-of-trainers approach that thereafter reached more than 6000 polling staff from all governorates, resulting in gender-responsive polling arrangements as per international standards concerning women's civil and political rights. In Mexico, ahead of their 2021 parliamentary elections, the seed funds to the CO were, for example, used to support the Electoral Institute of Oaxaca's innovative and culturally-sensitive communications campaign on preventing VAWP. The campaign included the production of guidance materials in indigenous languages and dissemination of such through social media and indigenous associated radio stations. Additionally, a specialised modular training was produced by the Local Electoral Institute, helping more than 180 indigenous and Afro Mexican female leaders and local public servants to enhance their capacities to engage in political life. Sida sees this as an important LNOB effort.
The reporting, furthermore, outlines a substantial number of knowledge products and tools that, in 2021, were developed, translated into different languages, and used, which offered UN Women's COs an important package of practical guidance and practice-informed research to support national programme implementation. E.g. a study on Effective, Decisive and Inclusive Women's Leadership in COVID-19 Response and Recovery (mapping lessons learned and recommendations), a Guidance Note on Preventing Violence Against Women in Politics (to COs and UNCTs on how to support Member States in addressing VAWP, including women HRDs, journalists, CSO activists), a Map on Women in Politics in 2021, etc. Also, importantly and for the first time, a comprehensive overview of women's political participation at the local level was provided within the working paper Women's Representation in Local Government: A Global Analysis by UN Women as the sole custodian agency for SDG indicator 5.5.1b. This is an important knowledge product as it aims to shift the global narrative from national to local decision-power, a less known but critical level of governance. A Women in Local Government website, an multi-year project, was also finalised and launched in 2021.
Harmonised data collection tools on VAWP, namely a series of questionnaires for officeholders, for political candidates, and for voters were developed, tested and implemented in 2021. These aim to fill a crucial knowledge gap in terms of measuring the magnitude of VAWP, identify the most frequent forms of and settings for such violence, what women are most a risk, who the main perpetrators are, what complaints mechanisms are used, etc. As a result of implementing these surveys, UN Women has generated the first ever comparable data on VAWP experienced by women, basically data on the aforementioned aspects, in five countries (Nepal, Jordan, Lebanon, Palestine and Tunisia). Sida sees this as another crucial knowledge product and tool.
Last, but not least under this outcome, UN Women's SPF reporting also provides an account of the important contribution the programme has to strengthening its own staff capacities on WPP. It outlines that in response to the corporate thematic evaluation on WPP (2018) which called for increasing thematic capacity in the field, SPF funding has helped UN Women to ensure that COs have recruited national experts to fill gender knowledge gaps and increase capacity on WPP within various institutions such as electoral management bodies. It has also ensured that there are now regional WPP advisors in Europe, Central Asia, and in East and Southern Africa, but also that the existing thematic presence on WPP in Latin America, the Caribbean and the Arab States has been strengthened. UN Women outlines how beneficial this has been in terms of being able to ensure localised expertise as well as rapid responses to fluid political developments. It has also helped in building the capacity of aspiring women leaders and candidates, focusing on LNOB. Sida sees this as very positive and in line with its' expectations and hopes for the SPF. UN Women, furthermore, outlines that having these regional advisers and thematic policy and programme staff, as well as flexible resources, has given UN Women the necessary institutional capacity to have a seat at the table when it matters the most, and to be able to respond to country-level requests with active support and guidance, even where UN Women is a non-resident agency.
Outcome 2.1: Gender responsive measures (mechanisms, processes and services) promote women's leadership and participation in politics.
Under this outcome, UN Women provides technical assistance, knowledge-sharing and capacity strengthening to parliaments, executive cabinets, and local legislatures to promote gender equality and womens empowerment. Moreover, womens political participation as candidates, voters, and elected leaders is strengthened, as well as womens leadership more generally, through capacity strengthening.
UN Women reports that 20 country offices have supported parliaments, ministerial cabinets and local legislatures to pass legislation and measures that promote gender equality. Parliamentary discussions on new laws on VAWP passed in Brazil and El Salvador, involving parliamentary women's caucuses and CSOs, were assisted.
Through SPF support over 3000 women leaders, aspiring candidates and elected officials in 19 countries enhanced their political leadership and networking skills in campaign planning, communications and messaging, constituency outreach and networking during 2021. More countries but less individuals were covered this year in comparison with last year (2020: more than 4000 individuals in ten countries). Specific examples and results are highlighted from Kyrgyzstan, Nigeria, Zimbabwe and Bolivia. The latter being the virtual training programme on Women's Political Rights and Young Leadership delivered to 259 young members of Municipal Youth Councils, designed and implemented by UN Women Bolivia together with the Vice Ministry of Equal Opportunities and the Plurinational School of Public Management (EGPP), which Sida visited during its field trip in March/April 2022. The training provided the young women with knowledge and tools to support their active role as promoters of peaceful political dialogue and agents of change for gender equality in their communities.
Important examples of results in terms of gender sensitive reforms adopted by political institutions, UN Women reports about the establishment of a National Observatory of Women in Politics in Brazil. The multi-stakeholder mechanism aims to investigate, monitor and centralise research on women's political representation at federal, state and municipal levels. Moreover, in Bolivia, 48 municipalities out of 137 targeted modified their internal regulations so that they reflect VAWP after having received training and technical assistance on Bolivia's law against harassment and violence against women in politics. In Jordan, the Royal Committee to Modernize the Political System has produced recommendations that include a new elections law (introducing Temporary Special Measures, TSMs), a new political parties law and related constitutional recommendations, as well as specific recommendations on how to improve local administration for women and youth's effective engagement in public life. Consultations on these recommendations provided a platform for dialogue with a wide range of stakeholders and raised awareness about the recommendations. UN Women also supported the Ministry of Political and Parliamentary Affairs (MOPPA) to organise a workshop with women parliamentarians and senators to discuss the recommendations which allowed the MPs to directly discuss these recommendations with the Minister and and the the members of the Royal Committee.
Outcome 3.1: Constitutions and legal frameworks to advance gender equality and women's rights are reformed and adopted.
Under this outcome, UN Women works to support constitutional and legal reforms. SPF continued to engage with field offices and UN partners to support the development and implementation of gender responsive legal frameworks and it continued to enable UN-Women to advance on the implementation of the Equality in Law for Women and Girls by 2030: A Multi-stakeholder Strategy for Accelerated Action.
Specifically in 2021, the SPF, through policy guidance, technical assistance and seed funding, contributed to the initiation of legislative reviews in Cote d'Ivore, Burundi, Central African Republic, Haiti, Mozambique and Zimbabwe. Also, a comprehensive legislative review was undertaken in five Caribbean countries: Trinidad and Tobago, the Bahamas, Barbados, Belize and Guyana. The aim of the reviews is to determine how the constitution, statutes, laws, administrative regulations, etc., specifically relating to women and girls, impact on the achievement of gender equality.
During the SPFII, UN Women provided seed funding to 19 countries that directly contributed to successful programming within legal and justice reform processes. Examples of seed fund results in 2021 include supporting UN Women's joint UN work with the Constitutional Convention (in charge of drafting the new constitution) in Chile aiming to mainstream gender in the constitutional reform, as well as supporting Egypt's National Council for Women's (NCW's) discussions with MPs leading up to the tabling of procedural revisions of the law that governs personal status affairs (which governs marriage, divorce, inheritance, child custody, etc.). In the latter case, several knowledge products were generated and the NCW has developed initial procedural revisions of the Family Law that will be submitted to the Cabinet in 2022. In Nigeria UN Women CO carried out of review of the constitution from a gender perspective, identifying numerous proposed changes that promote women's rights, and in Tanzania, the CO supported the Tanzania Women Judges Association (TAWJA) in designing a Gender Bench Book on Women's Rights that aims to ensure that the capacity of the judiciary to ascertain women's access to justice is strengthened. A directive was subsequently issued by the Minister of Constitution and Legal Affairs to the Judiciary to further use the book to strengthen prosecutors' and state attorney's capacity to handle cases in gender sensitive ways, especially cases that affect women and girls left behind like rights of persons with disabilities, those living with HIV/AIDS, young and elderly women.
Women, Peace and Security
Overall: In this part of the report some results and changes for the WPS agenda at large, and on a global longer term in relation to the Security Council is accounted and analysed in Annex B, in addition to the outcome and output based progress report. The in-depth piece includes a focus on occurred changes and the the role of UN Women and, to the extent possible, the SPF modality and strategic partnership. Furthermore, Annex D contains a brief on WPS and disability inclusion (as part of the Leave No One Behind approach) and gives a broader stock taking, despite not being SPF specific.
As previous years, the report under this outcome suggests a high degree of synergistic funding, where SPF has served as a catalytic instance to attract other funding mechanisms, and thus, contributed to a strong increase in overall WPS funding. The programme overall encompasses activities and deployments in 49 countries, five regional offices and expertise to five investigation missions.
Also during 2021, Covid-19 continued to take its toll, and paired with complex political and security challenges in many countries, this jointly hampered and even reversed impact of certain interventions during the period.
Outcome 4.1 Women, Peace and Security commitments and accountability frameworks are adopted and implemented in conflict and post-conflict countries
Under this outcome, a large part of the funding is designated for staff capacities as a method to enhance UN Women's WPS capacities at all levels, and in 2021 this translated into 28 long-term experts and 12 short-term, an increase from 2020 (22 and 9 respectively).
One key area of work is for UN Women to support countries production, adoption and implementation (also localization) of National Action Plans (NAP) on WPS. It is reported that to date, 103 countries have now adopted a National Action Plan on WPS, compared to the 37 which were in place when the first phase of SPF started. This work includes for example technical assistance, in-put on drafts, arrangement of consultations, trainings, gatherings of best practise and political advocacy. 12 countries adopted new plans in 2021, four of whom processed their first plan and received assistance from UN Women to do so, e.g. Malawi, Mexico, Peru and UAE and six countries who have processed but not yet adopted NAPs (Chad, Ethiopia, Libya, Tajikistan, Uruguay and Vietnam). The work on enhancing implementation of NAPs is also reported for a large number of countries (24) and localization efforts in an increasing number of countries, including for 2021 DRC, Kyrgyzstan, Iraq, Philippines, Sudan and Ukraine.
UN Women's work with NAPs was part of the corporate evaluation finalised in 2020, but disseminated in 2021, leading to stronger focus on supporting the implementation of plans instead of creating new ones. Below are some more specific samples of results and achievements:
Some high end results are reported as being part of the NAP processes, like the DRC government commitment to a 30 per cent quota for women in decision making bodies, or in Jordan, where the armed forces and the public security directorate adopted a first ever gender mainstreaming strategy which included the appointment of 77 gender advisers and focal points and six gender champions. Increased targets has been set for higher female representation in peace keeping, and a first all-female police unit was deployed to the UN mission in DRC.
The efforts to "localize" NAPs have in 2021 been the continued focus in the Philippines, Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao, resulting in 20 provincial government actions plans where women's involvement was strengthened in the work with security actors and former combatants. Also in DRC and Ukraine have the support to localized plans been reported a priority - the former including a SPF-funded expert deployed to the Eastern parts of the country in order to support a provincial NAP in Ituri, and the latter leading to eleven adopted local action plans in, the then, conflicts affected regions of Luhansk, Donetsk and Zaporizhzhia regions. As part of the set-up of a secretariat at steering committee for Niger, this resulted not only in a more whole-of government approach but also in operational and financial plans for all the regions in the country. In Iraq the process of a monitoring plan of NAP resulted in sectorial plans for all ministries and a specific plan for Kurdistan. And despite Mexico having its first NAP, the progress reported in terms of net work building of women peace builders have already resulted in integration in 11 states and 54 municipalities.
In other countries, like Armenia and Azerbaijan, the conflict dynamics between the countries in Nagorno-Karabakh have influenced amendment and review of respective NAP processes and UN Women reports that its support has been amended accordingly for stronger influence on gender integration in overall responses to the conflict.
It is important to take note of how sudden changes in conflicts alters the prerequisites, or lead to back lash and even reverse results, like in the case of Myanmar, a country which had very good implementation levels of its localization process in Mon and Kayin states before the military take over. But after February 2021, these processes had to be put on hold as women's organisations had to leave the country, offices were raided and staff detained and abilities to participate in any political conversations disappeared. Furthermore, military control of financial resources increased risks for both UN Women and its partners. The same dynamics is reported for the localization of NAPs in Blue Nile ad South Darfur in Sudan, after the military coup.
Another part of the work under this outcome relates to the global normative frame works and to strengthen global commitments. In this line, SPF continued to fund and serve as the secretariat for the WPS Focal Point network with its 91 members. The network enables a close coordination among Member States and create a space to periodically share and exchange lessons learned and best practices. In 2021 focus has particularly been on the enhancement of the knowledge hub. An important task for SPF globally has been to launch and serve the new WPSHA compact which was launched at the Generation Equality forum in 2021 and now has 160 signatories. The compact is set out as a voluntary mechanism to enhance for example coordination, implementation, monitoring and accountability of WPS commitments. SPF also continued to fund the secretariat function of the Informal Experts Group which is directly connected to the Security Council.
From the reporting (Annex B) an internal assessment elaborates on the changes in the Security Council and the impact the SPF has played for supporting progress over time. It constitutes an excellent example of how allowing a more analytical approach to the SPF, changes, transformation and real results can be elaborated and the reporting can move away from activity based reporting. This annex spells out what the SPF has contributed to, for example by serving as the secretariat to the Security Councils informal experts group on WPS, which has steeply improved the councils knowledge and deliberations. In addition, the SPF has enabled UN Women to engage with the SC with briefs, monthly meetings with council members, UN and civil society, participation of female briefer, collaborations, follow-up, advising and facilitating advocacy opportunities, including contribution to the NGO Working Group (receiving support directly from Swedish MFA). These measures jointly can be seen to a larger or lesser direct degree having influenced council decisions and its deliberations over the past ten years. Just a few numbered examples:
- Two thirds of SC resolutions have WPS language (compared to one third in 2010) and the quality, areas and details have improved a lot. In general, the tilt towards only having CRSV language has balanced out and includes the rest of the agenda like participation and leadership.
- Female briefers to the SC has increased immensely. Between 2000-2015 there were 25 in all, compared to 2021 when that reached 60 women. Before 2016 no women was ever invited to specific country specific meetings, which is now a routine practise and happens several times every month.
The short-term experts, which were deployed to investigate sexual and gender based violence, the level of documentation and evidence collection in line with international standards increased in Belarus, Ethiopia, Libya, South Sudan and Syria. It is noteworthy that the SPF-funding has been used as a "gap-filler" for these kind of tasks - and over the years the amount of experts used have been dependent on other funding sources. This could under other circumstances be perceived as a weakness, while in the case of SPF this is welcomed as Sida want this funding mechanism to work flexibly in favour of UN Women being able to fulfill all its mandates under the chosen thematic areas. In Belarus it has, for example, led to an revelation of how systematic SGBV has been used as torture against both women and men in detention, especially as punishment against protesters, pro-opposition and also with a specifics target to LGBTIQ (perceived) individuals. In the Tigray region in Ethiopia it could be proved that all parties to the conflict committed SGBV to the level of war crimes and crimes against humanity, and these findings now serve the new international commission of Inquiry.
In this section there are numerous examples of synergistic funding being mobilised out of SPF funded staff, both in terms of other donors but also when applying and pushing other funds and mechanisms (like the WPHF, PBF, MPTF:s etc) to increase gender commitments. Regionally, it is reported that the advisers often have key roles in these processes. In Latin America and the Caribbean the adviser has mobilised 9,5 M USD in 2021 and with a further 3 M USD to be confirmed, as she helped and professionalized processes for a large number of offices. And in West and Central Africa she contributed to 3 M USD in new resources and 10 M USD awaiting. At times the regional advisers also strengthens the national offices for certain tasks, like in Chad. But also other SPF funded specialists have supported funding proposals, for example in CAR, DRC and Ethiopia.
In some countries, where UN Women has a long-term and strong collaboration and partnerships on WPS, the results are oftentimes broad in scope and expands to a large variety and cross-cutting areas. An example is Lebanon where results are reported for greater gender parity in the armed forces as well as broad mobilization on quotas for political participation, advancement of NAPs etc. Also Colombia showcase a strong WPS portfolio, strategic collaborations and influence in central processes like the Truth Commission and UN Verification team, as well as monitoring of gender provisions of the peace agreement, grants for protection of women human rights defenders etc.
There are a few other examples in the report of SPF being instrumental when it comes to women's direct participation in peace related processes, like for pushing the women 35 per cent quotas in South Sudan Revitalized Peace Agreement, leading to actual women's representation increase at community levels despite in modest terms. Support was also given to women's participation in track 2 processes between government and SPLM in Sudan, bringing together various fractions of the latter to agree on WPS priorities later presented in the Juba negotiations.
Humanitarian Action and Disaster Risk Reduction
Overall: The progress report outlines a lot of results and is, furthermore, complemented by Annex C which have short summaries of country specific work.
Outcome 4.2 Gender equality commitments adopted and implemented in humanitarian action which includes disaster risk reduction and preparedness, response and recovery
Under this outcome the SPF funded short- and long term deployments of experts are contributing to integrating gender into humanitarian action and its various frame works, providing inter-agency training/capacity building, technical expertise, as well as activating some seed funding for project implementation. In 2021 this meant disbursing gender expertise to 87 per cent of the humanitarian cluster system (where UN Women is present) and refugee responses in over 40 country and regional contexts. UN Women also serves as an accountability and monitoring mechanism for gender commitments in humanitarian actions, partly as part of the Inter-Agency Standing Committee, IASC, set-up.
The report contains numerous accounts of instances where UN Women are active members and have the ambition to influence, like Humanitarian Country Teams (or its equivalent) and lead, or as co-lead, Gender in Humanitarian Action Working Group, and in Regional and Global Platform for Disaster Risk Reduction, DRR. As mentioned above, UN Women, reports on its continued work with the IASC Gender Accountability Framework report which is providing analysis on the compliance with IASC policy set gender commitments, standards and roles and responsibilities of 31 UN coordinated humanitarian response planning cycles. To this end, UN Women refers to outcomes which involves collaboration with other UN agencies, notably UNHCR, UNFPA and UN OCHA. As examples: a global MoU has been signed with UNHCR; the collaboration with UN OCHA (and IFRC) deepened in terms of promoting and normatively influence women's leadership in humanitarian settings; and a joint global partnership with UNFPA was initiated, resulting in a CERF global grant to UN-Women in November 2020 in six countries with a focus on GBV, both survivors and at risk populations.
Localization of the agenda has been an important approach and, for example, under the Grand Bargain frame work, UN Women produced three guidance notes on gender responsive localization, participation revolution and harmonized needs assessments. The guidance note on localization has been adopted by IASC.
Due to restrictions on travel, and in order to be cost-effective, UN Women refers to a new launch of a seven week training materials being converted into digital platforms - where access to gender in humanitarian program cycle can be increased.
Under the work of Disaster Risk Reduction and Resilience numerous results are reported, especially along the normative and coordination mandates where women's agency in these processes are at the core. As reported last year, gender was mainstreamed into the UN Plan of Action on Disaster Risk Reduction for Resilience 2015-2030 progress review. This led to a study and recommendations for the advancement of womens agency and leadership in disaster risk reduction. This has since informed the whole UN Plan of Action which is now to be monitored. During 2021 it is reported that UN Women has provided technical support to preparatory processes for the regional and global platforms for DRR, thus strategically advancing gender equality in this regard. At a high end, this resulted in the SG including a focus on closing the gender gap in DRR in the report on the implementation of the Sendai framework 2015-2030. Also, it is reported that the SPF funded DRR specialist supported the CEDAW General Recommendation (No 37) on gender related DRR in relation to climate change. At regional level this included the gender-responsive European Forum for DRR Roadmap (2021-2030) and Caribbean Regional Action plan.
Various materials and tools have been developed when it comes to gender-responsive DRR and resilience, in all cases in collaboration with other agencies like the World Bank, Unicef, EU and UNDRR. Synergistic funding between SPF and Australia has resulted in a Women's Resilience to Disasters Knowledge Hub, including a tracker of progress.
SPF funds continued to be used in order to build up a Women's Resilience to Disasters Programme and Humanitarian action in 2021. The approach has attracted other donors and its aim is to enhance womens agency and leadership for humanitarian response and disaster resilience in order to challenge gender-responsive norms, policies, strategies, systems, mechanisms and tools and standards globally. When it comes to building evidence and accountability, particular country examples are raised for the Asia and Pacific region as well as Vietnam, South Sudan, Haiti and Mexico, showcasing a broad samples of development of tool kits, analysis, studies, recommendations, forums and follow-up - mainly in line with the normative mandate at regional or national levels and often with a nexus approach and oftentimes as a collaboration with governments.
To enhance national and regional capacities, UN-Women provided dedicated gender expertise and technical assistance to Humanitarian Country Team members, particularly UN OCHA and the health cluster, on gender and humanitarian action, gender data, and to create an evidence base.
There are various examples provided, including the case of the refugee camp Cox´s Bazar in Bangladesh (where SPF funds the Head of office) where a broad strategic collaboration with the police, civil society, humanitarian actors and women's organisations has resulted in reinforced gender mainstreaming and women and girls in site management. In most reported cases UN Women provided capacity development or technical assistance of key partners (Asia Pacific, Fiji, Kiribati, Samoa, Tonga, Vanuatu, Solomon Islands, Myanmar, Nepal) often to the end of gender mainstreaming, developing tools, action plans etc. In some country settings, like the example of Lebanon, real time gender data was used to influence the humanitarian response not only nationally but also at regional and global levels, which is reported to have changed several policy decisions. In Palestine this work has led to an evidently stronger integration (and positioning in OCHA) of gender i humanitarian action. UN Women is working in partnerships and in Jordan, for example, to enhance a survivor centered approach to GBV, taking root in legislation and protection.
Organisational Effectiveness and Efficiency
UN Women reports that the findings of SPFIIs Mid-Term Review (MTR) have been fully addressed with 15 of the 17 key actions adopted in response have been completed, another 2 are no longer applicable. A direct result of the recommendations is, for example, the impact assessments of WPS and the Security Council. Sida sees this as positive given that all findings, by the closure of the activity period for this contribution, are handled.
Delivery in terms of finance and programmatic targets has been high since the inception of SPF and has increased, despite a dip due to Covid-19 in 2020.
